_meta.source: Approximate positions distilled from Erin Meyer (The Culture Map, 2014 scale charts), Geert Hofstede Insights country scores, GLOBE cluster research, and Richard Lewis culture-type model. Values are directional approximations for orientation, not precise measurements. Countries marked extrapolated=true are not in the original published sets and are positioned from their GLOBE cluster neighbours by the plugin authors.

meyer.eval: Evaluating: 0=direct negative feedback 100=indirect negative feedback (upgraders, third parties)
meyer.lead: Leading: 0=egalitarian (boss as peer) 100=hierarchical (boss as father figure / status distance)
meyer.trust: Trusting: 0=task-based trust (from competence/reliability) 100=relationship-based trust (from meals, time, family)
meyer.dis: Disagreeing: 0=confrontational (open debate is good) 100=avoids confrontation (open debate harms harmony)

highlights: Trust is task-based: competence, punctual delivery and follow-through build credit faster than dinners.
'How are you?' is a greeting, not a question; 'let's do lunch' is a friendly close, not always an invite.
Get to the point fast: conclusion first, then support (most applications-first culture on earth).
Positive framing expected: package criticism as 'opportunities'; blunt negativity reads as hostility.
Decisions come fast and are revisited just as fast — a signed agreement can be reopened by a new VP.
Litigation mindset: the written contract is the relationship's boundary.
Softer than the US on disagreement: upgraders and hedges ('perhaps', 'maybe we could') precede criticism.
Quebec behaves closer to Latin Europe: more relationship-oriented, longer lunches, more rhetorical flair.
Consensus-seeking is a national value; a decision imposed without consultation breeds quiet resistance.
Punctual, contract-respecting, but the relationship layer matters more than in the US.
High-context irony and understatement: 'quite good' may mean excellent; 'a bit of a problem' may mean disaster.
Indirect negative feedback via British humour and euphemism — decode the joke before responding literally.
Email formality: open with small talk, avoid first names until offered, sign off politely.
Class and school ties still lubricate trust; a shared alma mater beats a sharp pitch.
Decisions drift through meetings-before-the-meeting; the room rarely surprises the principals.
Storytelling and humour open meetings; skip the small talk and you seem cold, not efficient.
More relationship-driven than the UK: the pub conversation is part of the deal, not a distraction.
Criticism is wrapped; be careful not to read Irish politeness as full agreement.
Most egalitarian business culture: first names immediately, 'tall poppy' disdain for self-importance.
Direct, plain language; mock-modesty and self-deprecating humour earn trust, polish reads as waffle.
Debate is sport — disagreement is engagement, not hostility.
Like Australia but quieter and more consensual; consult stakeholders before announcing.
Maori protocols may open formal events — stand when welcomed, never speak over a mihi.
Modesty rules: overselling yourself or your company backfires.
Most principles-first persuaders in the West: method, logic and theory before conclusions — or you look lightweight.
Debate is intellectually valued; challenging your argument is respect, not attack.
The boss decides (grande école hierarchy); build the technical case for the cadre, not the crowd.
Lunch is business: relationship and hierarchy play out over the table, and August is dead month.
Criticism is direct in content, elegant in form; a French 'interesting' often means doubtful.
Split personality: Flanders leans Dutch (low-context, consensus), Wallonia leans French (hierarchical, rhetorical).
High uncertainty avoidance: bring structure, written follow-ups, and don't improvise the agenda.
Compromise culture — the country runs on coalition; expect negotiation to be slow but durable.
Relationships and bella figura first: who you are and how you present carries the deal.
Flexible time: meetings start late, run long, and interrupt each other — that is engagement, not chaos.
Formal titles and dress matter at first meeting; warmth and expressiveness build credit.
Northern and southern Italy differ sharply in pacing and formality — calibrate per city.
Personal relationship is the deal's engine: invest in sobremesa (the long table conversation after lunch).
Hierarchy with a human face: the senior person decides, but charm opens the door.
Scheduling is flexible and late dinner is a business arena; August and Christmas week are dead.
Face-saving matters — criticize privately, never across the table.
Among the world's highest uncertainty-avoidance: detail the plan, the contract, the contingencies.
Relationship-first and formal: titles (Doutor), patience, and family references build standing.
Group harmony over confrontation; a polite 'let's study it' can be a soft no.
Highest recorded uncertainty avoidance: reduce risk on paper and in person, repeatedly.
High-context, personal networks (gnosi) open doors that formal channels never will.
Lively interruption = interest; a silent Greek meeting is a failed one.
Most low-context communicators in the West: say exactly what you mean; euphemism reads as evasion.
Direct negative feedback is professional, not personal — do not soften, do not take offence.
Most linear schedulers: the agenda is a contract; being 10 minutes early is on time.
Principles-first: explain the method and the 'why' before the price, or you seem unserious.
Titles and order matter (Dr., Herr/Frau + surname); decisions are slow to form, then immovable.
Separate the person from the problem is NOT the local rule — criticism lands on the work, but relationships stay formal until you are invited in.
Punctuality is a moral value; late = disrespect, call ahead the moment you know.
Consensus across stakeholders before any announcement — surprise is a breach of process.
Modest, precise, understated: exaggeration destroys credibility instantly.
German/French/Italian cantons differ; match language and style to the region.
Formal and title-proud (Herr Doktor) despite low power distance scores — hierarchy is ceremonial and real.
More hierarchical and formal than Germany in manner; more consensual in structure.
Respect competence and order; small talk is thin, get to substance.
Bluntest feedback culture in the world: Dutch directness is candour, not rudeness — answer in kind.
Most egalitarian: everyone's view is heard regardless of rank; the junior engineer may shoot down your CTO.
Consensus (poldermodel) makes deciding slow, but implementation is fast and everyone is committed.
Calvinist modesty: splashing wealth or exaggerating marks you as untrustworthy.
Lunch is a sandwich at the desk; don't turn it into a relationship ritual.
Extreme consensus (samförstånd): decisions take many meetings but are then bulletproof — never force a vote early.
Flat hierarchy: the boss is a coordinator, not a commander; address everyone as equal.
Modesty law (Jantelagen): never claim to be better than the group; credit the team.
Work-life boundary is sacred: schedule meetings inside 9-4, never Friday afternoon; July is out.
Silence is comfort, not awkwardness; pause before answering shows respect.
Like Sweden but more direct and less ceremonially consensus-bound; friluftsliv small talk (cabin, ski) earns warmth.
Understatement and egalitarianism; titles are almost never used.
Trust starts high and is lost by behaviour — transparent, plain dealing wins.
Lowest uncertainty avoidance + low hierarchy: improvise, pilot, iterate — heavy planning reads as insecurity.
Hygge atmosphere in meetings: informal, humorous, first names, but decisions still go through consensus.
Humour is dry and pervasive; being able to take a joke is a trust signal.
Silence is communication: Finns pause long before answering — fill it and you lose standing.
Say what you mean, mean what you say: a Finn's 'maybe' is a real maybe, 'yes' is iron.
Sauna invitation is a relationship milestone; declining politely is fine, joining builds deep trust.
Less consensus theatre than Sweden; more quiet personal responsibility.
Formal hierarchy with hospitality: respect titles, expect warmth once invited past the formality.
High uncertainty avoidance: detailed contracts, contingency clauses, repeated written confirmation.
History made flexibility a survival skill — Poles improvise around rules while demanding them on paper.
Reserved until trust forms; initial formality and titles (pan/paní) are the entry ticket.
Skepticism is a cultural default — a Czech 'no' said with irony may be negotiable; a warm 'yes' may not.
Beer culture opens relationships; business stays formal longer than in Poland.
Pessimistic-precise communication: problems are stated first and plainly; optimism reads as naivety.
Status-conscious and formal at the table, but proud of technical excellence — lead with expertise.
High uncertainty avoidance + high masculinity: strong plans, strong egos, hard bargaining.
High power distance, relationship deals: the patron at the top decides; work the trusted introducer.
High-context yes: agreement may mean 'I hear you' — confirm in writing through the hierarchy.
Hospitality is generous and refusal offends; accept the coffee, the tuica story earns the contract.
Avtoritet rules: the senior person decides and being introduced to the right one is 80% of the deal.
Trust is personal and slow: banquets, toasts and dacha invitations are the real negotiation.
High-context and strategic: what is not said is the message; test statements against interests.
Extreme-range bargaining is normal — the first price is theatre; anchor and hold with warmth.
Contracts are a snapshot of the balance of power, not a final word; renegotiation is expected when power shifts.
Relationship-first: tea, meals and long personal talk precede business; rushing reads as disrespect.
Hierarchical and status-aware: meet the decision-maker, honor the pecking order, dress well.
Hospitality is a moral code — praise the tea, never criticize Turkey, and expect vigorous, friendly bargaining.
'Inşallah' framing on commitments: distinguish enthusiasm from a dated, owned promise.
Dugri (straight talk): interruption, challenge and bluntness are engagement — the most confrontational debating culture.
Chutzpah is admired; hierarchy is flat in practice (first names with the CEO), informal in dress.
Army-network trust: 'who did you serve with' opens doors; improvisation beats process.
Do not mistake argument for rejection — the shouting match often ends in a deal and a hug.
Wasta (connections) is infrastructure: the right Emirati sponsor or introducer changes everything.
Majlis protocol: coffee and extended courtesy talk open the meeting; never rush to the pitch.
Face is non-negotiable — a direct 'no' is rare; 'leave it with me' may be a polite refusal.
Friday-Saturday weekend; Ramadan working hours shrink and eating in public by day is banned.
Haggling is expected on almost everything except listed corporate rates; anchor high, concede slowly, keep warm.
The senior prince/family decision-maker is the deal; everyone else is a channel to him.
Majlis etiquette: accept dates and cardamom coffee (shake cup to decline refill), right hand only.
Personal trust over paper: multiple visits, family inquiries, and patience are the price of entry.
Never ask about wives, never show sole of shoe, never rush — time is divine (insha'Allah semantics).
Contracts flexible by design: terms are the start of a relationship, not its end.
Baksheesh and wasta culture: every process has a human key; tips and intermediaries lubricate.
Extreme high-context: listen for what is unsaid; a direct refusal is almost never spoken.
Politeness is lavish and commitments are soft — confirm everything in writing, gently, multiple times.
Bargaining is a social ritual with warmth; the first price is an invitation to a conversation.
Greeting ritual is the meeting: ask about family, health, journey — cutting it kills the deal.
Titles, rank and age rule: address Doctor/Chief/Engineer properly; elders speak first.
Relationship and community networks decide; the formal org chart is a shadow of the real one.
Flexible time ('African time'), loud expressive debate, warm persistence — but confirm, confirm, confirm in writing.
Generosity signals seriousness: hosting and gifts (modest, culturally apt) are read as respect.
Ubuntu ethos: identity is communal; decisions go through clan, church and community elders.
Greeting hierarchy strictly observed — shake hands in order of seniority, two hands for elders.
'Hakuna matata' surface calm over high-context reading; a soft answer often hides a hard no.
M-Pesa-first business culture: digital, mobile, relationship-brokered.
Two business cultures in one country: corporate English-speaking SA is Anglo-linear; township and traditional sectors are relationship-first and communal — read which room you are in.
Ubuntu reconciliation etiquette: consult broadly, acknowledge history, never dismiss elders.
Direct-ish but diplomatic; braai (barbecue) invitations are the relationship engine.
Load-shedding realism: build schedule slack; patience with infrastructure is a professional skill.
Jeitinho (improvised workaround) is a core skill: plans change, relationships absorb the shocks.
Personal warmth is the deal: physical proximity, first names fast, personal questions early.
Simpatía rule: never confront or embarrass; criticism is delivered obliquely or not at all.
Meetings run late and overlap; the conversation AFTER the meeting is where decisions actually happen.
Hierarchy with charisma: the patrão decides, but consensus-feeling is staged before it.
Personalismo: the person, not the company, is the deal — loyalty runs to individuals.
Respect for hierarchy and titles (Licenciado, Ingeniero); the senior man's presence signals seriousness.
Simpatía and face: 'yes' to be polite is common; verify real agreement through a trusted lieutenant.
Long relationship dinners, tequila toasts; refusing hospitality is refusing the relationship.
Time is relationship-elastic: arrive personable, never visibly impatient.
European-flavored Latin business culture: formal Spanish, style, and long meals matter.
Status-conscious and rhetorical; arguments are won with elegance as much as data.
Economic volatility made Argentines sophisticated skeptics: expect hard questions on downside scenarios.
Late dinners are business; noon meetings are coffee, not decisions.
Most formal and structured of LatAm: punctuality is respected, agendas followed, dress conservative.
High uncertainty avoidance: bring documentation, references, guarantees.
Reserved warmth: relationship still decides, but expressed through correctness and repeated contact.
Among the most collectivist cultures on earth: the family/network IS the organization.
Extroverted warmth, personal questions, small gifts — the relationship IS the contract early on.
Face and harmony: indirect refusal culture; read enthusiasm carefully and re-confirm quietly.
Titles and formality at first (Don/Doña), then rapid personal closeness.
Formal, hierarchical, relationship-first; the senior contact's blessing moves everything.
High uncertainty avoidance: slow trust, detailed paper, repeated visits.
Indigenous and business cultures interweave — respect for elders and community land sensibilities is practical, not optional.
Mianzi (face) is the currency: never correct a Chinese counterpart in public, even factually.
Guanxi (relational networks) is the operating system: banquets, favors and intermediaries precede terms.
The contract is the START of the relationship, not its conclusion — expect renegotiation as circumstances evolve.
'Yes' means 'I hear you', not 'I agree'; 'maybe' and 'it will be difficult' usually mean no.
Hierarchy is steep but decisions are consensual-under-the-boss: the team pre-aligns (the real meeting happens before the meeting).
Long-term orientation: they will trade short-term margin for long-term position; price patiently.
Gift protocol: give/receive with both hands, modest value (anti-corruption law is strict), never a clock.
Chinese face-and-relationship core wrapped in Anglo deal speed: fastest contracts in the Sinosphere.
Efficient, transactional surface over guanxi foundations — still relationship-gated underneath.
Cantonese dining etiquette at business banquets; respect seniority ordering at the table.
Softer, more indirect than mainland China: extra politeness layers, slower trust, deeper loyalty once won.
Consensus plus hierarchy: the boss decides after quiet alignment; give face to every senior person present.
Night-market banquet culture; gifting modest and gracious. Never discuss cross-strait politics.
Most consensual deciders on earth: nemawashi (root-binding) pre-aligns everyone — decisions are slow, execution instant, and a 'decided' thing never reopens.
Extreme high-context: the air between words carries the message; silence after your proposal is processing, not rejection.
Hierarchy is ceremonial and precise: meishi (card) exchange with two hands and a bow; seat order by seniority; never skip the visiting-card ritual.
Indirect refusal vocabulary: 'it is difficult', 'we will consider', silence — push for a clear yes and you force a face-losing no.
Perfectionism and risk-aversion (world-high UAI): bring exhaustive QC data, references, contingency plans.
Drinking (nomikai) is where the real consensus leaks out; never pour your own drink.
Punctuality is absolute — arrive 10 minutes early; the agenda is a covenant.
Fastest-moving Confucian culture: ppali-ppali (hurry-hurry) pace inside a steep hierarchy — decisions come quicker than Japan, with less consensus depth.
Kibun (mood/face) management: keep the atmosphere harmonious; causing a senior to lose face is fatal.
Titles and hierarchy are rigid: two-handed card exchange, senior speaks first, drinking rituals (never pour your own glass, turn away when drinking before elders).
Longest-term orientation recorded: they will lose money for years to own a market.
'We will review it' often means no; use a trusted intermediary to extract the real answer.
Hierarchy decides: deference to the senior person is expected; skip-level pressure causes silent sabotage.
Jugaad (frugal improvisation) mindset: flexibility is a virtue; the plan is a hypothesis.
High-context harmony: a direct 'no' is rare — 'we'll try', 'should be possible', or head-wobble = polite maybe.
Time is polychronic: meetings start late, are interrupted, and relationships stretch schedules — but deadlines for YOUR deliverables are enforced hard.
Relationship + family small talk opens everything; food hospitality is generous (respect dietary rules by community).
Bargaining is a sport: first quotes are anchors; warm persistence beats cold logic.
Deeply relationship-first (host-guest ethics): tea, patience, personal trust before any term sheet.
Family firms dominate: the patriarch decides; heirs execute; outsiders need a family-trusted introducer.
Islamic etiquette: right hand for giving/receiving, no alcohol at business meals, prayer-time pauses are normal.
Indirect refusals: 'In shaa Allah' on timelines separates intent from commitment — re-confirm concretely.
Personal introduction networks open every door; cold outreach rarely works.
Politeness overrides candor: confirm agreements in writing via a trusted local partner.
Hierarchy steep; decisions slow at the top, fast when the owner blesses them.
Ayubowan warmth with formal British-era manners: titles (Mr/Mrs) until invited otherwise.
Buddhist patience culture: unhurried meetings, indirect disagreement, gentle humor.
Hierarchy and family networks decide; Religious festivals (poya days) pause business monthly.
Lowest uncertainty-avoidance culture on earth combined with rule-following precision: quick to try new deals, strict about compliance (fines culture).
Efficient, low-drama, contract-clean East-West hybrid: the easiest Asian entry point, but relationship depth still decides the big accounts.
Multiracial etiquette: match Malay/Indian/Chinese protocols; halal awareness at meals is basic respect.
Kiasu (fear of losing out) drives sharp bargaining; decisions are pragmatic and fast by consensus of a small top team.
Highest recorded power distance: absolute deference to rank; never bypass or contradict a senior Malay in public.
Bumiputera/Malay-Chinese/Indian business ecosystems each with own norms — identify which network you're in.
Face and harmony: refusals come as 'boleh cuba' (can try); read commitment levels carefully.
Ramadan pacing, Friday prayers, no left-hand giving; halal dining default.
Pancasila consensus + musyawarah (deliberation-to-accord): meetings are long, courteous, and the decision emerges from socialization outside the room.
Face (jaga muka) is absolute: never say a hard no; indirect channels carry the real message.
Paternal hierarchy with the Bapak (father/patron) at the center — the patron's blessing IS the decision.
Patience with time ('jam karet' = rubber time); Ramadan and Lebaran shut business for weeks.
Right hand only for exchange; modest gifts accepted graciously; never show anger — composure is power.
Kreng jai (considerate deference) silences disagreement: a Thai team will warmly agree in the room and quietly not comply after — verify through allies, not confrontation.
Hierarchy with the boss as khun po (father figure): the senior person's nod matters more than the meeting's consensus.
Sanuk (fun) belongs in work: meetings with warmth and lightness outperform formal pressure.
Face protection: never lose your temper — visible anger marks YOU, not them, as the problem.
Wai greeting etiquette (press palms, slight bow) by seniority; never touch heads, never point feet.
Monarchy is sacred ground: zero jokes, zero commentary, zero exceptions (lèse-majesté is enforced).
'Up to you' often means 'please decide so no Thai has to refuse you'.
Confucian hierarchy with fast-dealing energy: the boss decides, but negotiation is vigorous, patient, and daily.
Relationship (quan hệ) through introducers and shared meals precedes terms; tea and toasts are contract infrastructure.
Face and harmony on the surface, hard bargaining underneath — the first price is an opening joke.
Yes may mean 'I hear you'; confirm specifics in writing without forcing public admission.
Growing faster than process: contracts get renegotiated as reality shifts; keep warm, keep logging.
Hiya (shame/face) and utang na loob (debt of gratitude) are the real contract: favors create binding obligations.
Pakikisama (smooth social fit): group harmony decides; the amiable consensus in the room may hide private objections surfaced later through a go-between.
Family-first business: the clan network is the org chart; a family elder's word outranks titles.
Warm, Filipino/English bilingual, US-style directness tolerated more than elsewhere in ASEAN — but never embarrass anyone publicly.
'Bahala na' fatalism on deadlines: add buffer, follow up personally, keep it light.
One of the most relationship-first cultures on earth: no meaningful deal without invested personal time — multiple meals, family inquiries, patience measured in months.
Noy-noy (take it easy) pace: deadlines are aspirations; pushing hard reads as disrespect, not efficiency.
Extreme harmony culture: direct refusal almost never happens; 'yes' = 'I acknowledge', silence or deflection = no. A trusted Lao intermediary is mandatory to decode.
Hierarchy + patronage: the senior official/director's private blessing decides; formal signatures follow informally settled reality.
Face is everything: never criticize publicly, never raise your voice, never force a cornered 'no'.
Baci ceremony and toasts build trust (accept them); monks and wats are honored; heads never touched.
Verbal > written: what the senior person says across the table outweighs the document that follows.
Gentle, formal, hierarchy-centered: Samdech/Achar titles honored; elders and monks greeted first, with a sompeah if expected.
Harmony over candor: indirect refusals; use a well-connected Khmer intermediary to learn the true position.
Patron-client networks decide; patience and modest gifts of respect (not inducements) sustain relationships.
Anade (reluctance to impose) culture: nobody will tell you a hard truth to your face; decisions surface through intermediaries.
Hierarchy and military-era caution: approvals concentrate at the top; process is opaque — verify everything through trusted partners.
Generous hospitality ethics; Buddhism frames the calendar and courtesy.
